blocks.text: **The task.** Find all **unique** triples in an array that sum to zero. The same triple must not appear twice in the output, in any order.
Note that `-1` appears twice in the input, and both are used in the first triple. But the triple itself must not be listed twice — that is the part that makes this harder than it looks.
Sort, fix the first element, two pointers on the rest. The real work is suppressing duplicates.
**`if (i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue;`** — if this anchor value was already used, every triple starting with it has been found. Skip it.
**`if (nums[i] > 0) break;`** — the array is sorted, so once the smallest of the three is positive, all three are, and they cannot sum to zero. Everything after is hopeless.
**The two inner skip loops** — after recording a match, walk past repeats of both values so the same triple is not recorded again.
Why sorting is doing double duty
Sorting enables the pointer movement rule *and* makes duplicate suppression a cheap neighbour check. Without it, avoiding duplicates would need a hash set of triples — more memory and more code.
**Time: O(N²)** — an O(N) scan inside an O(N) loop. Sorting's O(N log N) is dominated.
**Space: O(1)** beyond the output, or O(N) if your language's sort allocates.
